sections.h2: Who inherits a Texas house when the owner left no will?
sections.html:
Chapter 201 of the Estates Code names the heirs in a fixed order, so the house goes to relatives by a formula, not by what the family expects. The answer turns on whether the owner left a spouse, whether there are children, and whether the house was community property or separate property.

A relative who is entitled to a share becomes an owner the moment the owner dies, but the county records still show the dead person as the owner. Until the heirs are proven in a court order or a recorded affidavit, a title company will usually not insure a sale. That gap between owning and being able to sell is where most Texas families lose time.

sections.h2: What happens when there is a spouse and children?
sections.html:
It depends on which kind of property the house is. The code splits the estate into the community estate and everything else, and each follows its own rule.

For community property, the whole community estate passes to the surviving spouse when the deceased spouse had no descendants, or when every surviving child or grandchild is also a descendant of the surviving spouse (Sec. 201.003). If the owner had a child who is not also the surviving spouse's child, the owner's undivided half of the community estate goes to the owner's descendants instead, and it stays charged with community debts.

For separate property, a surviving spouse with children in the picture takes one third of the personal property and a life estate in one third of the land. The children share the other two thirds of the personal property and hold the remainder interest in the land (Sec. 201.002(b)). Ask a probate attorney who has to sign before a buyer can get clean title when a life estate exists.

sections.h2: How are the shares divided in each situation?
sections.html:
The table below tracks the statute text for the common family patterns. It does not cover every case, and the terms "land" and "personal estate" are the code's own words.

Texas intestate shares by family pattern, from Estates Code 201.001 to 201.003
Family situationWho takes
Spouse survives, community property, all children are also the spouse'sSurviving spouse takes the community estate
Spouse survives, community property, a child from another relationship existsThat child and other descendants take the deceased spouse's undivided half
Spouse and children survive, separate propertySpouse: one third of personal property and a life estate in one third of the land. Children: the rest
Spouse survives, no children, separate property, parent or sibling also survivesSpouse: all personal property and one half of the land. The other half of the land follows the kindred rules
Spouse survives, no children, no parent, no sibling or their descendantsSpouse takes the entire estate
No spouse, children surviveChildren and their descendants
No spouse, no descendants, both parents surviveEqual shares to father and mother

sections.h2: What if the owner had no spouse?
sections.html:
With no surviving spouse, the estate runs down a list of kindred in the order set by Sec. 201.001. Children and their descendants come first and take everything.

  • No descendants, both parents alive: the parents split the estate equally.
  • No descendants, one parent alive: half to that parent and half to the siblings and their descendants, or all to the parent if there are no siblings or sibling descendants.
  • No descendants, no parents: siblings and their descendants.
  • None of those: the estate divides into two halves, one for paternal kindred and one for maternal kindred, working through grandparents and then their descendants.

When a child has died before the owner, that child's own descendants step into the place the child would have filled. The code calls this per capita with representation (Sec. 201.101).

sections.h2: Do adopted children, half siblings and late-born children count?
sections.html:
Adopted children inherit from and through their adoptive parents as if they were born to them, including children a court treats as equitably adopted (Sec. 201.054). The birth parents and their kindred cannot inherit from or through an adopted child.

A child counts as a father's child for inheritance in specific cases: birth within a marriage as described in Family Code Sec. 160.201, a court decree, adoption, or a signed acknowledgment of paternity (Sec. 201.052). Someone who claims to be a biological child can petition the probate court, and the court must find it by clear and convincing evidence. A person must also have been born before the death, or be in gestation at that time, and survive at least 120 hours (Sec. 201.056).

Half siblings take half as much as whole siblings when both kinds inherit together, and a group made up only of half siblings each takes a whole share (Sec. 201.057). These rules can change who has to sign a deed, which is why an overlooked child is the main risk in a quick family sale.

sections.h2: How do heirs prove who they are so the house can be sold?
sections.html:
Texas offers several routes, and the right one depends on the estate. The Texas State Law Library describes the main choices, and each one ends with a document the county clerk can record.

  • Affidavit of heirship: a sworn statement filed with the county clerk. No court reviews it, and no law forces a title company or buyer to accept it.
  • Determination of heirship: a probate court hearing that names the heirs by order. It results in a court order naming the heirs.
  • Small estate affidavit: available only when the estate is within the dollar limit in Estates Code ch. 205, assets are enough to pay debts, and the court approves. A house other than the homestead is a problem here, because the chapter excludes real property except a homestead passing to a spouse or minor children.
  • Administration: the court appoints an administrator, who can later sign a deed.

A buyer who pays value and relies in good faith on a recorded affidavit of heirship that omits a child can still get good title (Sec. 201.053), though the heirs remain liable to the omitted child for the sale proceeds. That rule protects the buyer, not the siblings who signed.

sections.h2: What does selling an inherited house with no will look like?
sections.html:
A typical sale follows a short chain of steps. The order matters because each one supports the next.

  1. Get a certified death certificate and list every relative who could be an heir.
  2. Pick a route to establish title: affidavit, heirship hearing, small estate affidavit where it fits, or administration.
  3. Record the proof with the county clerk in the county where the house sits.
  4. Have every heir, or the court appointed representative, sign the deed or contract.
  5. Settle the property tax bill. Texas property taxes attach as a lien each January 1, so the unpaid balance travels with the house.

If an heir wants to claim the homestead exemption on the inherited home, the appraisal district asks heirs who are not on a recorded deed for an affidavit of ownership interest, the owner's death certificate, a recent utility bill, and any court record citation, as described on the Comptroller exemptions page.

faqs.q: If my parent died without a will in Texas, do I automatically own the house?
faqs.a: If you are an heir under Chapter 201, your interest passes at death, but the record title does not change on its own. You need a recorded affidavit, a court order, or an administrator's deed before a buyer or title company will treat the sale as clean.

faqs.q: Does a surviving spouse always get the house?
faqs.a: No. A spouse takes the whole community estate only when every child is also the spouse's child or there are no descendants. With separate property and children, the spouse gets a life estate in one third of the land and the children hold the remainder.

faqs.q: Can I use an affidavit of heirship to sell an inherited house?
faqs.a: Sometimes. It is a sworn statement filed with the county clerk, and no law makes a third party accept it. Many title companies ask for a court order instead when the family tree is unclear.

faqs.q: What if there is a child nobody listed?
faqs.a: The child can still claim a share. A buyer who relied in good faith on a recorded affidavit keeps good title under Sec. 201.053, but the heirs who sold must answer to that child for the proceeds.

faqs.q: Do siblings inherit if the owner had no spouse or children?
faqs.a: Yes, in the order the statute sets. Both parents alive take equal shares. If neither parent is alive, the siblings and their descendants take the whole estate.
